"Akimbo" describes a specific position of the arms. When someone's arms are akimbo, both hands are placed firmly on the hips (or waist), and both elbows are bent and pointing outward — away from the body. This creates a wide, open shape, almost like a pair of wings on either side of the torso.

Picture a football coach on the sideline, watching his team fumble a play. Hands on hips, elbows flaring out, chest forward. That posture is arms akimbo.

This is not a relaxed posture. Arms akimbo almost always communicates something charged — defiance, impatience, frustration, authority, or confident challenge. Think of a parent who catches their child sneaking in past curfew and stands in the hallway, arms akimbo, not saying a word yet. The body is doing all the talking. It is a pose that says I mean business or go ahead, explain yourself.

It is almost never a warm or friendly stance.

Less commonly, the word applies to the legs. Legs akimbo means the legs are spread wide apart or splayed out at angles — like a toddler who has collapsed on the floor in a heap, limbs flung in all directions, or a person lying on a beach with their legs sprawled outward carelessly.

This is the most important thing to know about how the word works: akimbo is a predicative adjective, meaning it always comes after the noun it describes, never before it.

  • ✅ "She stood with her arms akimbo." — correct.
  • ✅ "Arms akimbo, he blocked the entire doorway." — correct.
  • ❌ "She had akimbo arms." — this sounds wrong and is not standard usage.

The word almost always appears alongside "arms" — the phrase "arms akimbo" is by far the most common construction you will encounter.

In contemporary writing, some authors use "akimbo" more freely to describe objects or things scattered or jutting out in various directions — tree branches sticking out wildly, or furniture thrown about chaotically. This is an informal, extended use. Purists and strict usage guides reserve the word for limbs only. Knowing this distinction will help you read it correctly in any context.

• "The headmistress stood arms akimbo at the school entrance, watching every student file past."
  • "He leaned against the wall, arms akimbo, daring anyone to challenge his decision."
  • "The child lay on the grass, legs akimbo, staring up at the clouds."
  • "She stormed into the room and stopped, arms akimbo, scanning every face."

"Akimbo" is a vivid, somewhat literary word. You won't hear it in casual everyday conversation very often, but it appears frequently in novels, journalism, and descriptive writing precisely because it does the work of a whole sentence in a single word. Instead of writing "she put her hands on her hips and pushed her elbows out," a writer simply says "arms akimbo" — and the image is immediate and complete.

That efficiency, combined with the strong attitude it conveys, is exactly why good writers reach for it.
